title: Extreme gradient boosting trees with efficient Bayesian optimization for profit-driven customer churn prediction
venue: Technological Forecasting and Social Change (Elsevier; ISSN 0040-1625)
harvard_reference: Liu, Z., Jiang, P., De Bock, K.W., Wang, J., Zhang, L. and Niu, X. (2024) 'Extreme gradient boosting trees with efficient Bayesian optimization for profit-driven customer churn prediction', Technological Forecasting and Social Change, 198, 122945. doi:10.1016/j.techfore.2023.122945.
abstract_summary: The paper proposes BO-XGBT, an XGBoost churn classifier whose structural hyperparameters (learning rate, min_child_weight, max_depth) and, unusually, its class-weight parameter (scale_pos_weight, searched in [0.0001, 50]) are tuned by Bayesian optimisation (Probability-of-Improvement acquisition) directly on the Expected Maximum Profit criterion for churn (EMPC; Verbraken et al., 2013) rather than on accuracy, F1 or AUC. It is benchmarked on eight public Kaggle churn datasets from six sectors (e-commerce, telecom x3 including the IBM Telco set, bank, newspaper, insurance, Uber) against twelve BO-tuned comparators (CART, KNN, LASSO, MLP, Gaussian naive Bayes, random forest, grid-searched XGBoost variants, and the profit-driven B2Boost) using 10-fold cross-validation with a held-out validation fold and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests over 80 estimates. XGBoost variants yield the highest EMPC on every dataset; BO-tuned XGBoost significantly beats grid-searched XGBoost on EMPC (p = 5.5e-8) and is much faster when several hyperparameters are searched; optimising the class weight adds profit over both the default weight (CW=1) and a deterministic cost-based 'balanced' weight. The profit advantage does not carry over to AUC or top-decile lift. Sensitivity analyses over BO iteration counts and over CLV assumptions (EUR 100/200/300) show the results are stable.

claims_supported.claim: Tree ensembles (random forest / gradient boosting) achieve top or near-top ROC-AUC on telecom churn data, often close to logistic regression.
claims_supported.where: Supported for the first part; only indirectly for the 'close to logistic regression' part. Tables 5-6 (Section 5.1, pp. 19-20 of the preprint) report AUC on three telecom datasets: on the IBM Telco dataset (Dataset 2, n = 7,040, churn 26.55%) the XGBoost variants have the top AUC (GS-XGBT 0.8601; BO-XGBT 0.8544) with BO-random forest at 0.8565, and the text states 'all XGBT variants ... consistently outperform the other classifiers considered'. However, the paper has NO plain logistic regression benchmark; the nearest linear model is BO-LASSO (a LASSO-penalised linear model), which scores 0.8460 on the IBM Telco data (within 0.014 of the best tree ensemble) but about 0.06 lower on the two larger Cell2Cell-type telecom sets (Datasets 7-8: LASSO 0.616-0.617 vs XGBoost 0.674-0.678). Also, on the IBM Telco data even Gaussian naive Bayes reaches 0.8424, so all models are within 0.02 AUC there. Cite this paper for 'tree ensembles top the AUC ranking' but not for a direct comparison with logistic regression.

claims_supported.claim: Explainability (SHAP or similar) identifies contract type, tenure and monthly charges (or equivalent) as key churn drivers.
claims_supported.where: Not supported. The paper contains no SHAP, LIME, feature-importance or any feature-level analysis; no feature (contract, tenure, charges) is ever discussed as a churn driver. A full-text search of the preprint finds 'SHAP' only in the title of a cited reference (Chehreh Chelgani et al., 2021) and 'contract' only in the phrase 'multiple contractual settings' describing dataset selection (Section 4.1). The scout's note is correct that the paper offers no XAI content.

claims_supported.claim: Business or profit-oriented evaluation changes which model or threshold is preferred compared with accuracy-only evaluation.
claims_supported.where: Supported. The abstract and Introduction argue that classifiers 'optimized for accuracy-based performance measures ... may not always fulfill the critical business objective of profit maximization', and Section 2.2 says selecting hyperparameters on statistical indicators 'ignored the primary objective of the learning process'. Empirically, Section 5.1 states that XGBoost's EMPC superiority 'does not translate to other metrics, i.e., top-decile lift and AUC', and Tables 5-6 show the metric changes the winning model: e.g. Dataset 1 (GS-XGBT CW=balanced tops AUC at 0.9944 but BO-XGBT tops EMPC at EUR 9.10), Dataset 3 (GS-XGBT CW=1 tops AUC 0.8652, BO-XGBT tops EMPC EUR 7.38), Dataset 6 (GS-XGBT tops AUC 0.9464, BO-XGBT tops EMPC EUR 28.05); on the IBM Telco set BO-random forest has higher AUC than BO-XGBT (0.8565 vs 0.8544) but lower EMPC (EUR 10.64 vs 10.72). On thresholds/weights: EMPC is evaluated at the profit-optimal cut-off T (Eq. 3) and the profit-optimised class weight beats both the default (CW=1) and the 'balanced' cost-ratio weight, with the authors concluding that 'simply and deterministically setting class weight may degrade CCP performance'. Caveat: the paper does not report an explicit accuracy-chosen threshold versus a profit-chosen threshold side by side; the threshold effect is embedded in the EMPC/class-weight results.

claims_supported.claim: Any other specific finding this paper makes that would be useful for a critical discussion of churn prediction methods, imbalance handling, calibration, uplift, survival, fairness or deployment (state it precisely).
claims_supported.where: (a) Imbalance handling: treating the class weight (scale_pos_weight) as a profit-tuned hyperparameter outperforms both no weighting and the deterministic cost-based 'balanced' weight of Eq. 8; on most datasets the 'balanced' weight actually LOWERS EMPC relative to CW=1 (e.g. IBM Telco: BO-XGBT CW=balanced EUR 10.63 vs CW=1 EUR 10.67; insurance: 4.33 vs 4.45), i.e. naive re-weighting can hurt profit (Section 5.1, Tables 5-8). (b) On the IBM Telco dataset all 13 models fall in a very narrow band (EMPC EUR 10.36-10.75 per customer; AUC 0.842-0.860), so model choice matters little on that benchmark compared with the larger Cell2Cell-type sets. (c) EMPC parameterisation used: CLV = EUR 200, retention-offer cost d = EUR 10, contact cost f = EUR 1, acceptance probability c ~ Beta(6,14) (Verbraken et al., 2013 defaults); robustness checked at CLV 100/200/300 (Section 5.4, Tables 11-12). (d) Efficiency: BO with 100 iterations per hyperparameter (400 total) versus a 500-point grid; on the IBM Telco set BO-XGBT trained in 74.8 s versus 234.9 s for GS-XGBT, and 257.5 s vs 2,464.8 s on Dataset 7 (Table 9); BO-XGBT beats GS-XGBT on EMPC with Wilcoxon p = 5.5e-8 and beats BO-random forest with p = 1.2e-13 (Table 7). (e) Evaluation protocol worth emulating: 10-fold CV with a separate validation fold for tuning and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests across 8 datasets x 10 folds. (f) Gaps the student can critique: no probability calibration, uplift modelling, survival analysis, fairness or deployment/monitoring analysis; no interpretability; no plain logistic regression baseline; and the authors' own stated limitation (Section 6.4) that the CLV-to-retention-cost relationship is assumed rather than measured, so EMPC rankings depend on untested cost assumptions.
